title: ReVault – new secure archive format
summary:
reVault is a new, secure-by-default archive format called a lockbox, designed to be simple to use.

I've been working on reVault for about 2 years. It was originally written in Dart, but with the improvements in AI, I decided to port it to Rust using AI.

It's now in beta, so I'm looking for feedback, particularly around the different language bindings.

A lockbox is encrypted, signed and compressed by default. Each can be disabled selectively.

  - Hybrid post-quantum or passphrase encryption, including metadata.
  - Zstd compression.
  - Pure Rust libraries wherever possible.
We intend to phase out remaining C code as alternatives become available. The project has been scanned using OpenAI's Daybreak cyber security tools.

The manual is a work in progress: https://docs.revault.onepub.dev/

reVault supports Linux, macOS and Windows, x64 and arm64, plus Wasm. The core is Rust, with bindings for C/C++, Java, Dart, Python, Ruby, JS/TypeScript, Go, C#, Kotlin, Lua, PHP and Swift.

Within a lockbox you can store:

  - Files, directories, permissions and symlinks.
  - Variables.
  - Forms.
Variables, forms and the lockbox itself can have descriptions.

reVault uses a portable vault (just another lockbox with structured content) to hold your keys, contacts' keys, lockbox aliases and form definitions.

It ties into your platform's secure store, so logging into your desktop unlocks your vault. You don't have to enter a passphrase every time you access a lockbox. You can disable this.

There are lots of shortcuts. Creating a lockbox stores an alias in your vault, based on its filename or a name you choose:

  lbx create /some/path/mybox.lbox
  lbx mybox open --duration 1h
  lbx mybox var set KEY VALUE
Set a default lockbox and you can leave its name out:

  lbx session default mybox
  lbx var get KEY
You can mirror a directory tree into a lockbox and update it when the directory changes:

  lbx store.lbox mirrors project create --from ./project --to /projects/project
  lbx store.lbox mirrors update
The API lets you read, write and seek within files without extracting them to the filesystem. Each lockbox has a table of contents, so extracting a single file from a multi-gigabyte lockbox is fast.

Recovery

Updates are transactional, with automatic rollback for failed updates. The format is designed for recovery: content is stored in pages, allowing unaffected content to be recovered if part of a lockbox is corrupted.

Sharing

An encrypted lockbox is more useful if you can share it.

reVault has an open-source keyserver for exchanging public keys, with validation through a second trusted channel. It's still experimental.

OnePub has donated a server to run a single keyserver. If you're interested in donating resources, I'd like to bring up a second redundant server. It's pure Rust, uses under 100 MB RSS and supports rate limits.

To publish your default profile's public key:

  lbx vault profiles email you@example.com
  lbx vault profiles publish
Give the publish code to your contact. They can import your key:

  lbx vault contacts receive
Display your profile's fingerprint and exchange it through a second trusted channel:

  lbx vault profiles fingerprint
Repeat the process in the opposite direction to get their key. Once you have it, grant them access to your default lockbox:

  lbx access grant alice
You can then email the encrypted lockbox to Alice.

To install the CLI and get started:

  cargo install revault_cli
  lbx vault init
  lbx completion install
Completion installation detects your shell. To diagnose issues:

  lbx doctor
The language bindings are published to their respective package repositories.

I'm looking for constructive criticism of the project on its own merits, particularly the APIs and language bindings. I'm not interested in a debate about using AI.

title: Ask HN: Why a Great Product Won't Succeed Without a Community
summary:
I'm really tired, fed up, and angry. You can create the best product in the world, but people always choose what their favorite influencers tell them to. People don’t make their own decisions anymore; they always think whatever they’re told to think. It’s really frustrating to try to create something good—something better than what others are doing. And I’ve realized one thing: to achieve success, it’s better to have a community that follows you than to have a great product. If you want to launch a good product, you’re better off building a community first—it’ll make everything easier and faster. I don’t care what you think of this post—I just want to say what I feel.

title: Ask HN: Windows Signing for FOSS Projects
summary:
Hey, all. I'm wondering how people handle signing packages for Windows when your project is open-source and there is no budget for an expensive code-signing certificate.

I thought I had found a solution with SignPath's (https://signpath.org/) free certs for open source, but I ran into two snags with them.

- I can't use custom runners in my github workflow. I was using a larger runner (still github hosted, I just picked a larger size) to run my tests faster, and SignPath failed the job because it didn't recognize the runner name. So I would have to go back to a standard runner with a name they recognize, which runs my tests about 3x slower.

- I have to approve each package signing, which means that a release process that was fully automated now has a step I have to manually approve.

I raised both of these issues with SignPath over a week ago, and I have yet to get a response, or to even have my signing certificate issued. So I'm about to give up on them.

Windows is only about 10% of my user base, so right now I'm leaning towards just continuing to not sign my Windows releases. But before I throw in the towel, I wanted to ask if anyone here knows of a better way to handle this.

Oh, and shameless plug for my project, a kubernetes management app: https://github.com/luxury-yacht/app/

title: Game trips modem/router breaker
summary:
Running Empire of the Ants on Steam Machine, this game (and only this game) does one of the strangest things I've ever experienced with any software: somehow, it trips the breaker feeding my router and modem. Frankly, I don't understand how this is possible, but it is reproducible. My first thought was that it was causing a power surge on the SM itself, but that's a different breaker. My second thought was that somehow it was triggering a load on the router and/or modem. The router and modem are connected to wall power through a UPS, so the game continues to play normally. I used the UPS display to show me output wattage but I didn't see a spike.

No other game on the SM, and no other console or device has ever done this and the situation is at once horrifying and fascinating. My only other thought is that the UPS is reacting to a stray Wifi signal originating with the SM and increasing load, triggering the breaker. But AFAIK the UPS is not set up to interact with Wifi at all, and frankly this seems very unlikely. I'm posting this in the hopes that someone else is experiencing something similar and we can get to the bottom of this mystery. And I thought of the HN crowd because I know we all love the "my software only crashes when it rains" type stories.

title: Ask HN: Kimi Code hit its 5-hour limit after $1.37 of API usage
summary:
I paid $19 for Kimi Code to test K3.1 Pro Standard (not Highspeed) using the official CLI v2.3.1.

I ran two tasks on small repositories:

1. Recommend movies based on an existing movie database. 2. Analyze a website's codebase.

Neither task completed. The entire 5-hour quota was exhausted within minutes.

I analyzed the actual session logs, including background agents:

- Fresh input: 368,203 tokens - Cached input: 1,183,744 tokens - Output: 39,324 tokens - Total: 1.59M tokens

At Kimi's published API rates, that's just $1.37 worth of usage before hitting the 5-hour limit which is easily less than 5% of what Claude Code offers at $20 subscription.

The logs show: "429 You've reached your 5-hour usage limit."

For comparison, Claude Code on a $20 subscription processed roughly 381M tokens over 4-5 hours using Opus 5.5 xhigh, mostly cached input. That's not a controlled benchmark, but the difference in usable capacity is staggering.

Both Kimi tasks failed without delivering results. I have video evidence and detailed logs, but won't publish private repository data.

Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=hSr-DLn88AM

Is this a quota-accounting bug, or are Kimi's $19 subscription limits intentionally this restrictive?

Disclosure: I also develop a competing coding agent. These tests used Kimi's official CLI.

title: Bring arc features to any browser. Here's how.
summary:
Fellow Arc users as you are on a journey to find a new place to settle in, i thought i should share this unique new thing you can try. I was also an Arc user since it was invite only. so i understand your pain.

Last year on my journey of moving on, I started working on a sidebar called SupaSidebar inspired from Arc built natively for macOS, in August 2025.

It attaches to any browser and brings cool features from Arc like: - Spaces, Folders to keep things like links, files and folders separate - Fuzzy search current open tabs, browser history and saved links - Air Traffic Controls to route links to correct browser/profile - Global shortcuts + drag and drop to save stuff - Search directly in websites using command panel - Auto Archive (still in beta) - iCloud Sync

Also its unique spot as a app makes these awesome things possible: - See open tabs from all browsers in a single sidebar - Backup and export to never lose your tabs - Saved links can be opened in any browser/profile - Common browser history across browsers (Private. Stays on device.) - Save Finder files and folders - Command panel is highly advanced

I am open to chat over email anytime and very very interested in finding ways to make it more useful to other Arc users.

Let me know if you'd like to try it out, would be happy to share the link to website. It has a free forever version upto 3 spaces with all the features.

ps: you can checkout video by Fernando Anselmi on youtube "Best Alernative to Arc Browser in 2026". He explains issues he faced moving from Arc and how he found a way through SupaSidebar and other browsers. Not Sponsored, found it existed few days back.

title: PSA: Do not use term "vibe coding"
summary:
... because it is hopelessly vague and useless.

What does it mean? "Forget that the code even exists AND fully give in to the vibes"? What vibes? How are vibes defined? Are one supposed to dance freestyle on a flat plain? This ain't agentic engineering, that's for sure.

It seems the original coinage was connected to a thought of an AI-led WYSIWYG environment; perhaps connected to a new type of library repository, and managed under a novel source code control system that may or may not be a hard fork of Git. This is much closer to agentic management and graph engineering, but that was not the road the other term took later.

And it certainly doesn't matter now. The best models now are good at doing everything from scratch, uncannily and frighteningly good. So good that there is now a risk of corporate AI budgets no longer growing simply because there won't be anything left to automate in a year or two, tanking the valuation of many decacorn startups and setting up very precarious times ahead.

---

Just my thoughts.

I needed to publish myself.

title: Ask HN: Linux at work revoked due to MDM, how to fight?
summary:
I'm a software engineer that likes Linux.

My employer is going all in on their B2B strategy. We're implementing full mobile device management. I just got news that I will need to hand in my laptop EOY and get a Mac instead.

I'm of course a little upset. I had a verbal agreement with my former manager (he has quit) that I would get a Linux laptop when I signed.

I'm not sure what the best way to make my case is. I don't want to be combative (Linux or I quit!). I don't want to make the IT department lose face by questioning them picking a MDM vendor without Linux support.

Has anyone been in this situation? All help appreciated!

Workplace: used to be a unicorn startup, did some layoffs. about 500~ people now. A handful Linux users (1%)

summary:
